The agent interoperability protocol landscape, as captured by 2024-2026 literature, is characterized by significant institutional convergence and technical maturation, primarily centered around MCP, A2A, ACP, and ANP. The Linux Foundation formalized this consolidation in December 2025 by launching the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as a neutral top-level foundation [0]. The AAIF hosts MCP, A2A, and related infrastructure [0]. This 2025–2026 institutional convergence also covers the protocol layer, including MCP, A2A, and ANP [3], [6].

The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, introduced by Google in April 2025, targets enabling communication and coordination among AI agents themselves [2]. A2A is an open protocol, developed in collaboration with over 50 partners [2]. Its goal is to allow AI agents, built on different frameworks and by different vendors, to communicate [2]. Google donated the A2A specification to the Linux Foundation in June 2025, simultaneously launching a broader project structure for agent interoperability standards [5]. By August 2025, the competing Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), initiated by IBM Research and later backed by Cisco, merged with A2A under the same umbrella [0], [5]. This merger consolidated what had been three competing standards into one [0]. A2A has matured through a parallel institutional and technical trajectory [5]. The protocol advanced from v0.3.0 in July 2025, which introduced streaming-first transport and enhanced Agent Cards with capability negotiation, to v1.0.0 in January 2026 [0]. Version 1.0.0 marked the transition from experimental to production-ready status, introduced signed Agent Cards for cryptographic verification, and codified discovery and trust mechanisms [0]. As of early 2026, A2A Agent Cards were deployed by more than 50 organizations participating in the AAIF working group [0], [1]. This deployment provides the first credible cross-vendor agent interoperability deployment in three decades [1]. A2A adopts a lightweight, web-native approach with declarative discovery and interoperability built in, similar to how HTTP functions for web servers [5]. It handles peer communication and assumes decentralized discovery through Agent Cards [8].

The Multi-Agent Communication Protocol (MCP) standardizes the agent–tool, or vertical, interface [1]. MCP addresses an agent’s interaction with its environment, including data and tools [2]. It opts for a pragmatic, JSON-based description using Agent Cards to facilitate discovery [5]. MCP’s structured tool interface assumes the calling agent knows which tool to invoke, lacking built-in discovery [8]. Adjacent specifications have begun to fill gaps outside MCP’s core scope [2]. WebMCP, accepted as a deliverable of the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group in September 2025, extends MCP into browser-native execution [2].

MCP and A2A address complementary needs within the agent interoperability landscape [1]. MCP focuses on agent-to-tool interaction, while A2A focuses on agent-to-agent interaction [1], [2]. The common deployment pattern involves an orchestrator agent that delegates subtasks via A2A while invoking tools via MCP [1]. Platforms such as AutoGen, LangChain, and CrewAI provide the orchestration scaffolding for this pattern [1]. AWS Strands and Microsoft Semantic Kernel are early platform-level integrations supporting both protocols [1].

The Agent Network Protocol (ANP) is also identified as part of the protocol layer in the 2025–2026 institutional convergence [3], [6]. Ehtesham et al. [24] specifically compare MCP, A2A, and ANP [3]. The "Agent Network Protocol Technical White Paper: Towards an Open Internet of Agents" was published in 2025 by Agent Network Protocol Contributors [4].

The most commonly discussed trade-off across these protocols, particularly between MCP and A2A, lies in their target relationship or scope of interaction. MCP is designed for vertical interaction between an agent and its tools or environment, assuming prior knowledge of the tool to be invoked [1], [2], [8]. In contrast, A2A is designed for horizontal peer-to-peer communication and coordination among agents, incorporating decentralized discovery mechanisms [1], [2], [8]. This distinction highlights a functional specialization rather than a direct trade-off of features within the same domain. A common limitation, rather than a trade-off between them, is that neither MCP nor A2A natively addresses trust, pricing, or accountability [1]. These gaps drive further institutional work [1].

Within this framework, models iteratively revise their responses based on a set of predefined, human-crafted rules, referred to as constitutions [DOC 2]. This revision process can be repeated over multiple iterations, enabling the model to reflect on its outputs using randomly selected constitutions [DOC 2].

However, the literature also surfaces disagreements regarding the optimal conditions for when reflection helps versus hurts, particularly when compared to alternative feedback mechanisms. Work described in [DOC 2] indicates that diverse peer feedback combined with memory can outperform self-critique [DOC 2]. This method supplies agents with dynamic peer feedback grounded in their own mistakes, requiring no human input [DOC 2]. This approach enables more targeted refinement and outperforms Self-Critique with the same number of revision steps [DOC 2]. Furthermore, the addition of Long-Term Memory (LTM) significantly enhances debate performance relative to Self-Critique [DOC 2].

Despite the observed superiority of peer feedback with LTM, Self-Critique initially achieved lower error rates on HarmBench compared to debate scenarios without memory [DOC 2]. For example, Self-Critique recorded a 15.36% error rate versus 21.0% in SReD for the first triad in debate scenarios lacking memory [DOC 2]. This suggests that while self-critique is a valuable mechanism for iterative improvement and learning from past errors, its effectiveness can be surpassed by multi-agent peer feedback, especially when integrated with long-term memory systems.

The 2024-2026 agentic-RAG literature indicates that hybrid retrieval, which combines lexical and dense retrieval with reranking, often outperforms dense-only retrieval under specific conditions, particularly when a balance between precise term matching and broader semantic alignment is required [DOC 0]. Systems such as Agent KB (Tang et al., 2025d) and MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) exemplify this approach by integrating lexical and semantic retrieval to achieve this balance [DOC 0]. MIRIX further demonstrates this by performing retrieval from multiple memory databases for each query and concatenating the retrieved contents, prioritizing comprehensive memory access [DOC 9].

Hybrid search and blended RAG approaches have been shown to improve RAG accuracy (Sawarkar et al., 2024) and overall retrieval performance in RAG pipelines (Monigatti, 2024) [DOC 2]. The application of rerankers or query expansion substantially reduces the missing rate, especially in top-3 retrieval settings, with improvements ranging from 4.9pp to 11.4pp, thereby narrowing the gap between top-3 and top-5 retrieval [DOC 5]. A practical system employing hybrid search, combining dense (vector search) and sparse (keyword search) retrieval to identify top-10 relevant documents, followed by a reranking model to consolidate results, achieved significant performance gains in latency and precision [DOC 6].

Furthermore, in the context of agent memory, which differs from standard RAG corpora due to coherent interaction streams and substantial overlap in events and wording, dense-only similarity top-k retrieval often returns repetitive memories [DOC 3]. This becomes problematic when an answer depends on subtle updates or factual differences among otherwise similar interactions [DOC 3]. In such scenarios, hybrid retrieval with reranking is better suited to distinguish decisive evidence hidden among highly similar histories [DOC 3]. A diagnostic framework study on LoCoMo (Yuan et al., 2026) found that the retrieval method, including hybrid reranking, is a dominant factor, with average accuracy spanning 20 points across different methods, highlighting the potential for significant improvements with advanced retrieval strategies [DOC 7].

However, the literature also identifies situations where hybrid retrieval, or its advanced components like reranking and query expansion, does not consistently beat dense-only retrieval, or can even degrade performance [DOC 5]. It is noted that improved retrieval does not always ensure improved downstream outcomes [DOC 5]. The performance gains from advanced retrieval strategies are not uniform across different models [DOC 5]. For instance, with the Qwen model, query expansion under the top-5 setting actually degraded retrieval performance [DOC 5]. This suggests that the effectiveness of query expansion is critically dependent on the quality of the model responsible for generating the reformulated queries [DOC 5]. Moreover, except for GPT-4o at top-3, introducing advanced retrieval strategies can further reduce downstream performance [DOC 5]. This reduction is likely attributed to the inclusion of semantically similar but noisy entries, indicating that models can be sensitive to misleading or corrupted inputs introduced by these advanced methods [DOC 5].
